newsitem.title: PERU: Peru mediators to meet with rebel hostage-takers.
newsitem.headline: Peru mediators to meet with rebel hostage-takers.

text.p: Roman Catholic Church and Red Cross mediators prepared on Thursday to meet with Marxist rebels holding 72 captives at the Japanese ambassador's home in a bid to jump-start talks to end the 51-day-old Lima hostage crisis.
Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani and Red Cross representative Michel Minnig were due to enter the residence at 10:30 a.m. (1530 GMT) to meet with guerrilla leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini.

Government negotiator Domingo Palermo told reporters late on Wednesday that the meeting was aimed at restarting preliminary face-to-face talks, broken off since Dec. 28, between the government and the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).
Hostages, MRTA rebels and security forces passed a largely uneventful night without the gunfire and singing duals of recent early mornings.
Police beefed up their presence around the residence early on Thursday, sending motorcycles with flashing lights wheeling around nearby streets, but reduced their numbers before dawn, witnesses said.
On Wednesday, the government sent a military plane roaring over the residence and police checked security at a nearby house selected for a possible meeting between Palermo and Cerpa.

Speaking on local radio, Cipriani said on Wednesday that recent informal talks with Cerpa, conducted amid a climate of "respect and mutual trust," had given rise to "alternatives" to resolve the crisis. He did not elaborate.

But he called on both sides to ease tensions and tone down the war of words that has characterised the standoff since the MRTA burst in on a cocktail party and seized the residence on Dec. 17, taking some 500 guests hostage.

"It would help to improve the language, improve attitudes, and thus manage to quickly advance the start of talks," he told Radioprogramas del Peru. He also urged an "inner change in the positions of both parties."

Both sides have refused to budge on conditions for talks. The MRTA wants to put on the agenda its main demand that Peru release more than 400 jailed comrades, something the government has dismissed and refuses even to discuss.
On Wednesday, President Alberto Fujimori said his government was seeking to restart talks, organising meetings on "logistics" and between Palermo and guarantors named to observe the negotiations.
"We then hope to define the sequence of these preliminary conversations (with the MRTA)," he told reporters during a visit to a Lima shantytown.

The MRTA has released most of the nearly 500 VIP captives it seized seven weeks ago. But it has held onto its most valuable hostages, including two government ministers, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, nearly two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen and Fujimori's younger brother Pedro.
Although he has flatly rejected the main rebel demand, Fujimori has raised the possibility of easing harsh prison conditions and allowing the hostage-takers to seek asylum abroad.

During a five-day overseas tour, Fujimori received kudos for his tough handling of the crisis but promised Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in Toronto last weekend that he would resume direct talks with the MRTA.
Returning on Tuesday, Fujimori stopped briefly in the Dominican Republic, raising speculation the Caribbean nation may provide a refuge for the 15 MRTA fighters holed up in the residence.
Fujimori plans to travel to London this weekend to take part in an economic forum, government sources said.
